intro.content_html:
ʿAlī ibn Sulaymān al-Muqaddasī (fl. late 11th – early 12th c.) and his Commentary on Genesis

Who was Ali?

ʿAlī ibn Sulaymān — known in Hebrew as Eli ben Shelomo (ʿEli ben Solomon) and in Arabic as Abū ʾl-Ḥasan ʿAlī ibn Sulaymān al-Muqaddasī, "the Jerusalemite" — was one of the last great Karaite scholars of medieval Jerusalem. He flourished in the closing decades of the eleventh century and continued working into the early twelfth; a note in his own hand is dated to 1103 CE.

His teachers were the leading Karaite intellectuals of late-eleventh-century Palestine and Egypt. Jeshua ben Judah (Yeshuʿah ben Yehudah, Abū ʾl-Faraj Furqān ibn Asad) was probably his master in Bible. Sahl ben Faḍl al-Tustarī (Yashar ben Ḥesed), the Karaite theologian, composed his treatise Maqdisiyyāt in answer to questions Ali had put to him — so he was, in effect, Ali's master in kalām (speculative theology). Ali himself produced a stream of works: four Pentateuch commentaries, a Psalms commentary, a famous Hebrew lexicon called al-Agrōn (for which contemporaries knew him as ṣāḥib al-agrōn, "the man of the Agrōn"), a Karaite legal compendium, philosophical-theological tracts, and an anti-Islamic polemic. Almost everything he wrote was an abridgement (Arabic: intizāʿ, ikhtiṣār, mukhtaṣar) of earlier Karaite work. His gift was synthesis, not invention.

Sometime before the First Crusade reached Jerusalem in 1099, Ali left the city — almost certainly for Fustat (Old Cairo), where Karaite scholarship was beginning to take root. He was among the last of the avelei Tziyon — the "Mourners of Zion," the Karaite community that had made Jerusalem the spiritual and intellectual center of Karaite Judaism for two centuries. With the Crusader sack, that community ended. Ali's writing carries the world that produced it.

What is the Commentary on Genesis?

The text translated here is the Genesis portion of one of Ali's four Pentateuch commentaries — specifically, the intizāʿ ("digest") he made from Abū ʾl-Faraj Hārūn's abridgement of Joseph ibn Nūḥ's commentary on the Pentateuch. Hārūn, in the early eleventh century, had himself abridged Yūsuf ibn Nūḥ's late-tenth-century original. Ali's autograph manuscript survives in two pieces — Russian National Library Yevr.-Arab. I 4423 and Jewish Theological Seminary 9334 — and the Genesis section was edited and published by Solomon L. Skoss in Philadelphia in 1928. Skoss's edition is the base text for this translation. What we read is therefore three layers deep: a tradition of Karaite Bible-reading that began with Ibn Nūḥ, was honed by Hārūn, and reached us in the form Ali gave it.

How the commentary works

The commentary is selective. Ali does not gloss every verse — he stops where he has something to say. Of Genesis's fifty chapters, he treats twenty-eight. He skips most of the genealogical material, the second half of the Flood narrative, large stretches of the Abraham and Jacob cycles, and most of the Joseph story.

What he treats, he treats in a single recurring pattern:

  • A Hebrew lemma is quoted (e.g., bereshit — "in the beginning").
  • A gloss follows in Judeo-Arabic, often introduced by wa-qawluhu ("and his saying"), al-aqrab ("the closer [reading]"), or qīla… wa-qīla ("it has been said… and it has been said").
  • A dialectical question-and-answer may follow in the form fa-in qīla… kāna al-jawāb… ("if it be said… the answer is…"). This is the Karaite masʾala — the rationalist genre of weighing one possible reading against another. It is the heart of Karaite exegesis.

The voice is dense. Ali presupposes a reader who knows the Hebrew text well, who is comfortable with Arabic grammatical terminology, and who is ready to follow a fast-moving argument. Some passages are extended masʾala-style discussion; some are short grammatical or lexical notes; a handful are a Hebrew word followed by a single Arabic gloss.

The Karaite intellectual frame

Ali wrote within the Karaite engagement with Muʿtazilite rationalist theology — the speculative tradition that anchored Islamic and Jewish kalām in this period. Several characteristic Karaite positions surface in the Genesis commentary:

  • A rejection of al-ṣarfa — the Muslim theological claim that the Qurʾān's inimitability comes not from anything in the text itself but from God's "diverting" people from being able to compose its like. In the Babel pericope (Genesis 11), Ali argues that human language and human intellect themselves bear the marks of divine ordering.
  • A rejection of transmigration of souls, also at Genesis 11, where Ali considers and dismisses the doctrine.
  • A pre-existent-sin theodicy, especially at Genesis 18 — the proposal, associated with Muʿtazilite-leaning Karaites, that apparent injustices in earthly life resolve in a moral economy that takes prior states of the soul into account.

These are not asides. They are how Ali reads the text. Where the Hebrew Bible raises a question that Karaite kalām has addressed, Ali brings the kalām answer into the commentary.

How this edition was made

The translation was prepared from Skoss 1928. The editorial principles are simple:

  • Preserve Ali's voice. We render his parataxis as parataxis, his short sentences short, his dialectical structure intact. We do not smooth.
  • Preserve his quirks. Ali sometimes cites a verse by its number when he means a nearby verse; he sometimes refers to an earlier verse as coming "after" a later one; he sometimes lights on a textual reading that disagrees with the Masoretic text we know. We preserve every such case as he gives it and flag each in a footnote, so the reader can see Ali's text rather than a corrected version of it.
  • Footnote for context, not correction. Footnotes explain technical Arabic terms, situate sectarian arguments, identify quoted authorities, and note manuscript lacunae. The translation stays out of the way.
  • A glossary for recurring terms. Many of Ali's technical terms — ḥukm, maʿrifa, dalāla, ʿilla, naqḍ ʿāda — recur dozens of times. We define each once in the Glossary sheet and refer back to it from the footnotes.

Manuscript lacunae are marked with […]. A paragraph break in Ali's manuscript is noted with "End" on the relevant row. Where a chapter contains only a Hebrew lemma with no surviving Arabic gloss — at Genesis 37:1 and Genesis 44:18 — we render the lemma and explain the absence in a footnote.

Errors and corrections

If something looks wrong, it may be intentional — please check the footnote before flagging it. If after that you still believe there is an error, please write to info@thekaraitepress.com.

Sources for this introduction

  • Miriam Goldstein, "ʿAlī b. Sulaymān al-Muqaddasī," Encyclopaedia of Islam Three (Leiden: Brill, 2012).
  • Michael G. Wechsler, "ʿAlī ibn Sulaymān," in Encyclopedia of Jews in the Islamic World, ed. Norman A. Stillman (Leiden: Brill).
  • Miriam Goldstein, Karaite Exegesis in Medieval Jerusalem: The Judeo-Arabic Pentateuch Commentary of Yūsuf ibn Nūḥ and Abū al-Faraj Hārūn (Tübingen: Mohr Siebeck, 2011), pp. 38–44.
  • Meira Polliack, The Karaite Tradition of Arabic Bible Translation: A Linguistic and Exegetical Study of Karaite Translations of the Pentateuch from the Tenth and Eleventh Centuries C.E. (Leiden: Brill, 1997).
  • Solomon L. Skoss, ed., The Arabic Commentary of ʿAli ben Suleimān the Karaite on the Book of Genesis (Philadelphia: The Dropsie College for Hebrew and Cognate Learning, 1928).

glossary.content_html:
Glossary

Recurring technical Arabic vocabulary in Ali's footnotes. Compiled from 615 footnotes across all 28 chapters.

TermArabicDefinition
A. Kalām & theology
al-taklīfالتكليف"[legal] obligation" The kalām category of acts that fall under divine command rather than mere permission. The cluster of doctrines around taklīf is the central Muʿtazilite-Karaite ethical framework Ali presupposes throughout.
taklīf lā yuṭāqتكليف لا يطاق"an obligation that cannot be borne"; the classical category of "imposition beyond capacity," rejected as theologically impossible by the Muʿtazila (and so by Ali).
al-mukallaf / al-mukallafīnالمكلَّف / المكلَّفين"The [morally] obligated, the one legally charged, the [responsible] agent." The standard Muʿtazilite designation for the class of rational creatures upon whom religious obligation falls.
qādir and mutamakkinقادر and متمكِّنA paired kalām formula for the preconditions of moral accountability: qādir is "capable" (granted the ability to act), mutamakkin is "enabled, in firm possession of the power to act" (unobstructed in the exercise of that ability). Together they constitute the kalām conditions that must be satisfied before taklīf can rightly attach to an agent.
al-ʿādaالعادة"[established] custom / regular course of nature" The kalām term for the ordinary order of nature as God's habitual mode of acting (al-ʿādāt al-ilāhiyya). For Ash'arites this language replaces nature-causality outright; for the Muʿtazilī-leaning Karaites the picture is softer, but the regularity is still a divine habit, not an intrinsic necessity.
naqḍ ʿādaنقض عادة"breach of custom"; the standard kalām/uṣūl designation of the miraculous as a punctuated interruption of the regularity God customarily maintains.
al-ṣalāḥالصلاح"right action, [moral] soundness" In the Muʿtazilite kalām that informs much Karaite theology, the ethically right course of action. Distinguished from al-aṣlaḥ (الأصلح), "the [ethically] optimal" — the doctrine that God must will the most salutary outcome for His creatures.
al-taʿlīlالتعليل"providing the rationale, [stating the] efficient cause" The uṣūl al-fiqh term for indicating the legal reason behind a ruling. Karaite hermeneutics widely admits taʿlīl of biblical commandments where the text yields a discernible rationale.
al-shubhaالشبهة"[evidential] doubt, [the appearance of warrant]" The uṣūl al-fiqh category of the apparent-but-unsound reason that mitigates culpability. An agent acting under genuine shubha is not held fully responsible for what would otherwise be a wrong.
al-tawfīqالتوفيق"[divine] success-granting, [the] gracious-aid" The kalām term for the divine assistance that conduces to the agent's right action — contrasted with khidhlān (خذلان, "abandonment"), God's withholding of that aid.
ʿilm / ʿulūmعلم / علوم"knowledge" / "[branches of] knowledge" Propositional knowledge; in some contexts the cognitive faculties God implants. Often paired or contrasted with qudar (قُدَر), the [granted] capacities for action — the standard kalām pair: God endows each mukallaf with the ʿulūm and qudar required to discharge what He commands.
manzilaمنزلة"rank, station" Technical kalām term for the moral-ontological status of an agent. The Muʿtazilite slogan al-manzila bayna al-manzilatayn ("the position between the two positions") refers to their intermediate status of the grave sinner — neither believer nor unbeliever. Ali uses manzila generally for moral standing.
qabīḥقبيح"[ethically] ugly, [morally] foul" The Muʿtazilite-Karaite category of objective moral wrongness — paired with ḥasan ("[ethically] good"). Acts are qabīḥ in themselves, not merely because God has forbidden them; this is the cornerstone of the Muʿtazilite-Karaite rejection of divine-command voluntarism.
al-rasūlالرسول"the messenger" Ali's regular designation for Moses, usually with the honorific ʿalayhi al-salām "peace be upon him."
B. Hermeneutics & epistemology
ḥaqīqa and majāzحقيقة and مجاز"literal / figurative sense" The fundamental Arabic-rhetoric/uṣūl pair: ḥaqīqa is the primary lexical sense of an expression; majāz the metaphorical or extended sense. A central Karaite hermeneutic distinction, developed especially by Abū l-Faraj Hārūn.
al-ẓāhirالظاهر"the plain [sense], the manifest reading" The surface meaning of the text. Standardly contrasts with al-bāṭin ("the hidden, interior") and with majāz.
taʾwīlتأويل"interpretation, esoteric reading" The principled departure from al-ẓāhir when reason or another verse forbids the literal reading. Karaite taʾwīl is reason-constrained: it is admissible only where it is required, never as a default-mode of reading.
samʿ / ʿaqlسمع / عقل"revealed report / reason" The Karaite-Muʿtazilite epistemological distinction between truths accessible to the unaided intellect (ʿaqlan) and those given only by authoritative transmission (samʿan). Many religious obligations (e.g., specific ritual forms) are samʿī; the existence of God and the wrongness of injustice are ʿaqlī.
sharʿīشرعي"legal, [pertaining to] revealed Law"; the technical pair lughawī / sharʿī (lexical / legal) is a standard Karaite analytic distinction for whether a term's reference is fixed by language or by revelation.
al-aqrabالأقرب"the most plausible [reading]" Ali's signature marker for his own preferred reading after surveying alternatives. Contrasts with baʿīd (بعيد) — "improbable, far-fetched."
qiyāsقياس"analogy" The rule of regular morphological/conceptual parallelism — central Karaite hermeneutic-grammatical category. Where attested, an analogical inference is guaranteed by the regular pattern, even where not directly attested (adverb: qiyāsan قياساً, "by analogy").
dalālaدلالة"[conventional] indication" The kalām/uṣūl term for the relation by which an expression indicates its meaning. Ali invokes dalāla in arguments that God cannot speak ambiguously where comprehension is required: the very purpose of revealed address presupposes a stable dalāla — and so [[taʾkhīr-al-bayān]] is ruled out in the strong form.
taʾkhīr al-bayānتأخير البيان"delaying of clarification" The uṣūl al-fiqh problem of whether a divine pronouncement may issue ambiguously and only later be clarified. The Karaites and the Muʿtazila reject this in the strong form: any ambiguity at the time-of-need would be a defect in divine speech.
istithnāʾاستثناء"[an] unstated condition, [implicit] exception" The uṣūl al-fiqh term for an unspoken qualifying clause that, if operative, would restrict an otherwise unconditional pronouncement. Ali uses istithnāʾ to argue that some apparent divine breaches of promise are actually the operation of an implicit conditional.
mafsadaمفسدة"corruption, [thing that] produces harm" The legal-theoretical category of an act that yields net evil. Paired conceptually with maṣlaḥa (مصلحة) — the act that yields net benefit.
amāraأمارة"sign, indicator" The diagnostic feature by which one identifies a particular semantic value of a polysemous form. Used by Ali both for textual signs (an amāra in the verse pointing to one reading over another) and for evidential signs in argument.
fī al-taḥqīqفي التحقيق"in actual fact" Pairs with al-ẓāhir as the level of underlying truth opposed to the surface impression. Where the ẓāhir of a verse says X but fī al-taḥqīq the matter is Y, Ali is signaling that the apparent reading is misleading.
maʿrifaمعرفة"[discursive] understanding" In kalām: the cognitive grasp of a particular, often distinguished from ʿilm (propositional knowledge). Watch the polysemy: in grammatical contexts (e.g., Gen 9:228) maʿrifa means "[grammatically] definite" — a noun made determinate by the article, construct, or pronominal suffix, as opposed to nakira (نكرة, "indefinite").
masʾalaمسألة"question, dialectical problem" The Karaite dialectical-question marker that opens a hypothetical objection answered below. Closely linked to the in qīla / kāna al-jawāb formula (see Dialectic).
C. Grammar (naḥw)
fiʿl mā lam yusamma fāʿiluhuفعل ما لم يسمَّ فاعله"A verb whose agent is not named" — the standard Arabic-grammar term for the morphological passive (e.g., ḍuriba). Karaite grammarians use this designation for the Hebrew niphal / puʿal / hophʿal forms.
wāw al-ʿaṭfواو العطف"the vāv of conjunction" The standard Arabic-grammar designation for the coordinating vāv, taken over for Hebrew morphology. To be distinguished sharply from the nāqila (see below).
nāqilaناقلة"transferring, [tense-]shifting [vāv]" The Karaite grammatical doctrine of the vāv-conversive that toggles the apparent tense of a Hebrew verb. See al-Kāfī §§ on this device. The vāv is one of Ali's standing concerns; he is careful to distinguish wāw al-ʿaṭf from nāqila even when the surface form is identical.
ẓarfظرف"temporal/locative adverb" The Arabic grammatical category of the temporal complement — equivalent to Hebrew mafʿūl fīhi in Abū l-Faraj's typology.
waṣfوصف"descriptive attribute / qualifier" The Arabic-grammar term for a qualifying expression. In analyzing an iḍāfa (genitive construction), interpreting the dependent term as a waṣf means it describes the head's own quality rather than relating it to a distinct entity.
jinsجنس"genus, generic kind" Pairs with nawʿ (نوع), "species, particular kind." A foundational distinction for class-membership arguments.
al-ḍamīrالضمير"the pronoun" The Karaite-naḥw term covering both independent and bound pronouns — including bound personal-elements of verb prefixes and pronominal suffixes whose antecedent must be identified.
amrأمر"imperative" The standard Arabic-grammar term, applied here to Hebrew morphology.
ḥukmحكم"rule, regulation" The regular syntactic/semantic behavior of a lexeme. Watch the polysemy: ḥukm also means "ruling, judgment" (as in Gen 9:228 where Hebrew ba-adam is read as a substantive denoting human judicial agency).
taqdīrتقدير"supplied/virtual reading" The standard Arabic-grammar term for grammatically-required elements that must be understood without being expressed. Adverb: taqdīran (تقديراً), "by way of supplied/virtual reading" — as a notional supplement rather than as an actually-asserted reality. (Ali also uses taqdīr in its lexical sense "proportioning, measuring out," especially when recovering the etymological sense of khalq "creation" from classical Arab lexicography.)
qiblaقبلة"acceptance, [direction-of-prayer]" The Qurʾānic/kalām term for the place to which acceptable prayer is directed. Ali uses qibla in this hierocentric sense in his treatment of Abraham's altar (Gen 22) and Jacob's stone (Gen 28).
maḥaṭṭمحطّ"central [clause], [pivot] point" The rhetorical/syntactic term for the load-bearing element of a multi- clause expression — the clause on which the meaning ultimately settles.
D. Dialectical signature formulae
qīla / wa-qīlaقيل / وقيل"it is said / and it has been said" Introduces an attributed prior view (often one Ali will reject). Cf. CONVENTIONS § Karaite signature formulae.
in qīla … kāna al-jawābإن قيل … كان الجواب"if it be said … the answer is" The two halves of the Karaite masʾala (problem-and-answer) dialectic: a hypothetical objection followed by Ali's reply. The masʾala dialectic is the unit of argument throughout Ali's commentary.
yajrī majrāيجري مجرى"runs the course of, functions as" Ali's signature subsumption-formula bringing a Hebrew construction under a categorial rubric. Inflected forms: yajrī majrāhumā "runs the course of the two of them" (used for paired constructions).

content.hebrew: Gen 1:1
content.english: Gen 1:1

content.hebrew: בראשית ברא אלהים – אפתתח תע׳ תוראתה בדׄכר אלכׄליקה̈ למא כאנת [א]ול אלאכׄבאר ואפאדנא מן תרתיבהא מא לם [נסת]דרכה עקלא אדׄ אלעקול דלת עלי חדתׄ אלע[אלם] במא פיה מן דון אלתרתיב ואלתפציל אלמסתפאד שרעא
content.english: "In the beginning God created" (bereshit bara Elohim). He (may He be exalted) opened His Torah with mention of the creation, since it was the foremost of [its] reports; and He has conveyed to us, through its arrangement, what we could not have apprehended by reason alone — for the [human] intellects testify to the world's having come into being on the basis of what is in it, [even] apart from the [particular] ordering and detailed account that is supplied by revelation.

content.hebrew: וקו׳ בראשית – יקתצׄי מחדׄופא גיר מדׄכור ליכון מתׄל בראשית ממלכות (ירמיהו כו:א) וגירה פקיל אן אלמחדׄוף מנה דׄכר אלזמאן יעני פי אול אלזמאן כׄלק אללה אלסמא ואלארץׄ ודׄלך פאסד אדׄ אלזמאן הו חרכאת אלפלך ולם יכן חינידׄ אלפלך מכׄלוקא.
content.english: "In the beginning" (bereshit). [This] requires an elided element¹, not explicitly stated, so that it might be like bereshit mamlekhut "in the beginning of [the] kingdom" (Jer 26:1) and the like. It has been said² that what is elided is the mention of time — that is, "at the start of time God created the heavens and the earth." But this is faulty³, since time is the motions of the celestial sphere, and the sphere had not yet been created at that point.
content.comments: ¹ maḥdhūf (محذوف) — "elided" element supplied to complete the construction. Ali's hallmark construction is yaqtaḍī maḥdhūfan (يقتضي محذوفا), "[the verse] requires an elided element." ² qīla (قيل) — "it is said"; introduces an attributed prior view, often one Ali will reject. ³ fāsid (فاسد) — "faulty," stronger than "flawed"; signals a logical defect in the proposed reading.

content.hebrew: וקיל אן מענאה פי אול חאל ודׄלך בעיד איצׄא אדׄ אלחאל אקל אלאוקאת ווקת לם יכן תחקיקא למא תקדם דׄכרה. פאן עני הדׄא אלקאיל באלחאל תקדירא לא תחקיק פלא דליל עלי אנה תע׳ כׄלק אלסמא ואלארץׄ פי חאל דון חאלין ומא זאד ענהמא אדׄ אלעקל לך יקץׄ בה ולא נץ עליה אלסמע ואיצׄא פאנה אדׄא כאן מעני אלחאל ואלוקת סוא ואל[ו]קת לא יכון אלא חאדתׄא פכדׄלך אלמוקת בה אדׄ אלוקת לא יכון וקתא ללקדים תע׳ ולא יכון אלקדים עז וגל וקתא לגירה למא אסתחאל אלחדותׄ עליה פינבגי אן יכון הנאך חאדתׄין א׳ וקתא לכׄלק אלסמא ואלארץׄ והו אלדׄי ענאה הדׄא אלקאיל בקו׳ פי אול חאל כׄלק אללה אלסמא ואלארץׄ.
content.english: And it has been said that its meaning is "in the first state"¹ — but this too is far-fetched², since a state³ is the briefest of moments — a time⁴ that has not [yet] truly come about, by what was just said. If this speaker means "state" virtually⁵, not actually, then no proof remains that He (may He be exalted) created the heavens and the earth in [some] one state to the exclusion of two, or in addition to them — since neither reason stipulates this nor does revelation textually attest it. Moreover, if the meanings of "state" and "time" are equivalent, and a time can only be a created thing, then likewise what is timed by it [must be created] — since a time cannot be a time for the Eternal (may He be exalted), nor can the Eternal (mighty and majestic) be a time for any other, since coming-into-being is impossible for Him. So there must be two created things there: one [that is] a time for the creation of the heavens and the earth — which is what this speaker meant by his words "in the first state, God created the heavens and the earth."
content.comments: ¹ fī awwal ḥāl (في اول حال) — "in the first state." ² baʿīd (بعيد) — "improbable," lit. "far"; Ali's standard term for an interpretation he judges unlikely. Contrast yaqrub (يقرب) and al-aqrab (الأقرب). ³ ḥāl (حال) — in Abū l-Faraj's terminology (and so Ali's), the primary sense is "present tense" (Khan/Gallego/Olszowy-Schlanger 2003 §3.0); here it carries the related sense of "present instant / state." ⁴ waqt (وقت) — "time," a discrete moment. ⁵ taqdīran (تقديرا) — "by way of supplied/virtual reading," as a notional supplement rather than as an actually-asserted reality. From taqdīr (تقدير), the standard term for grammatically-required supplied elements.

content.hebrew: ואלאכׄר כׄלק אלסמא ואלארץׄ והו אלמוקת פמא הו דׄלך אלחאדתׄ אלדׄי כאן וקתא לכׄלק אלסמא ואלארץׄ. אלי תרי אן אלקאיל יקול פי אול [ח]אל מן אחואל אשראק אלשמס צלית פיגׄעל א׳ וקתא ואלאכׄר מוקתא בה למא כאנא חאדתׄין. וקד ימכן כון אלאמר פיהמא באלעכס בחיתׄ יגׄעל אלוקת מוקתא ואלמוקת וקתא כאן יקול אשרקת אלשמס אול צלאתי. ואדׄא כאן דׄלך כדׄלך פאלאקרב אן יקאל פי בראשית מע אול מכׄלוק כׄלק אללה אלסמא ואלארץׄ לאן אלבא כמא תעמל מע אלשי איצׄא נחו הלחם בעמלק (שמות יז״ט) אלדׄי הו במתׄאבה̈ הלחם עם עמלק נטׄיר להלחם עם בית ישראל (מלכים א׳ יב:כא) וליס כון עמלהא מע מגׄאזא במאנע מן הדׄא אלקול אדׄ אלחקיקה̈ פיהא קד אמתנעת.
content.english: And the other [created thing] is the creation of the heavens and the earth — which is the thing-timed. So what was that created thing that served as the time for the creation of the heavens and the earth? Do you not see that one might say, "In the first of the states of sunrise I prayed" — making the one [the state] a time and the other [the prayer] timed by it, since both are created? It is equally possible to reverse this, making "the time" the thing-timed and "the thing-timed" the time — as when he says "the sun rose [at] the start of my prayer." If that is so, the most plausible¹ reading of bereshit is "together with the first thing created, God created the heavens and the earth" — for the bā² (= the prefix preposition ב) functions also with the sense of "with," as in hillaḥem be-ʿamaleq (Exod 17:9), which is equivalent to hillaḥem ʿim ʿamaleq, parallel to le-hillaḥem ʿim bet yisraʾel (1 Kgs 12:21). And the fact that the bā's bearing the sense of "with" is figurative³ does not bar this reading, since the literal sense⁴ is in this case excluded.
content.comments: ¹ al-aqrab (الأقرب) — "the most plausible"; Ali's signature marker for his own preferred reading after surveying alternatives. ² bā (با) — the Arabic name for the prefix preposition بـ; Ali uses it to refer to the Hebrew prefix ב, treating the two as functionally equivalent. ³ majāz (مجاز) — figurative or non-literal usage. A central Karaite hermeneutic category, developed especially by Abū l-Faraj. ⁴ ḥaqīqa (حقيقة) — literal or true sense, paired with majāz.

content.hebrew: ואלדליל אלעקלי אקתצׄא אן לא יכון כׄלק אלסמא ואלארץׄ סאבקא לכׄלק חי ינתפע בכׄלקהמא לכונה עבתׄא פלא בד מן כׄלק מלך קבל כׄלקהמא או מע כׄלקהמא יעתבר בדׄלך וה[ו] אלמעני בקולנא מע אול מכׄלוק כׄלק אללה אלסמא ואלאר[ץׄ] וקד יגׄוז אן יקאל פי דׄלך בעד אול מכׄלוק לאן אלבא קד תעמל איצׄא בעד כקו׳ שנה בשנה (שמואל א׳ א:ז) אלדׄי מענאה סנה̈ בעד סנה̈. פאן קיל אלא גׄאז תקדים כׄלק אלעאלם אלדׄי ה[ו] נפע עלי כׄלק אלחי אלמנתפע בה כמא יכון פי אלשאהד אסתעדאד אלמנאפע תם אחצׄאר מן ינתפע בהא. כאן אלגׄואב. לאן גרצׄה תע׳ בכׄלק אלעאלם נפע אלאחי[א] בה עאגׄלא ואגׄלא פמתי כׄלי וגׄוד אלנפע מן וגׄוד אלמנתפ[ע] בה לם תחצל אלבגיה̈ וצאר תקדם אלכׄלק לא פאידה̈ פיה פיגׄב לדׄלך תקדים איגׄאד אלחי עלי איגׄאד אלעאלם או מקארן לה ואנמא חסן מא דׄכרתה פי אלשאהד למא תעדׄר עלי מסתעד אלמנאפע אסתעדאדהא ואסתדעא אלמנתפע בהא מעאמן חיתׄ יחתאגׄ פי דׄלך אלי אוקאת מתראכׄיה̈ ולמא לה איצׄא מן אלסרור ולדׄלך קדם אלואחד מנא אלאראדה̈ אלתי הי עזם עלי פעל אלמראד למא לה פיה מן אלסרור ותסהיל אלפעל בתכריר אלעזם ותוטין אלנפס עליה וקד תנזה תע׳ ען מתׄל דׄלך פי מראדאתה.
content.english: The rational proof¹ entails that the creation of the heavens and the earth cannot precede the creation of a living [being] who benefits from their creation — for [otherwise their creation] would be futile. So there must be the creation of an angel² prior to or together with their creation, who can take cognizance of [the creation] thereby. And this is what is meant by our saying "together with the first thing created, God created the heavens and the earth." One may also say bereshit means "after the first thing created" — since the bā also functions in the sense of "after," as in shanah be-shanah (1 Sam 1:7) meaning "a year after a year." If it be said: Surely the creation of the world — which is the benefit — might precede the creation of the living being who benefits from it, just as in the empirical case³ one prepares benefits and then summons the one who will enjoy them? The answer⁴ is: His purpose (mighty and majestic) in creating the world is to benefit the living [beings] by it, both presently and in the future; whenever the existence of the benefit is detached from the existence of the one who is to benefit, the desired end is not attained and the prior creation has no [further] point. Hence it is necessary that the bringing-into-existence of the living [being] precede the bringing-into-existence of the world, or coincide with it. What I just described in the empirical case is appropriate only because the one preparing the benefits cannot prepare them and summon their beneficiary together — these matters require intervals of time — and also because of the pleasure he takes in [the anticipation]. For this reason, one of us may put forward his desire⁵ — which is a determination upon the act of [whatever] is desired — because of the pleasure it brings him and because repeating the determination eases the act and settles the soul upon it. But He (may He be exalted) is beyond [needing] such a thing in His desires.
content.comments: ¹ al-dalīl al-ʿaqlī (الدليل العقلي) — "the rational proof"; standard Muʿtazilite-kalām designation for an argument grounded in reason rather than in scripture. ² malak (ملك) — "angel"; here, the rational agent whose existence the rational proof requires alongside or prior to the inanimate world. ³ al-shāhid (الشاهد) — "the empirical / witnessable"; the realm of human experience, used analogically (and then critically disanalogized) for the divine. ⁴ al-jawāb (الجواب) — "the answer"; the second half of the Karaite masʾala (problem-and-answer) dialectic. ⁵ irāda (إرادة) — "will, desire"; technical kalām term for the determination preceding an act. The argument here is that human anticipation/repetition of irāda eases action — a need Ali insists has no analog in God.

content.hebrew: וקולה ברא – יפסר כׄלק במעני יצר. אלי תרי אלי קו׳ ויברא אלהים את האדם (בראשית א:כז). וייצר ייי אלהים את האדם (בראשית ב:ז) גיר אן לשון יצירה ישתרך פיה אלקדים עז וגׄל ואלמחדתׄין כקו׳ ענה יוצר הארץ ועשה (ישעיה מה:יח). וענהם קאל יוצרי פסל כלם (ישעיה מד:ט) לכנה יפסר פיה תע׳ מן אלכׄלק ופיהם מן אלתצויר לרפע אלאיהאם עלי אן אצל אלכׄלק פי לגה̈ אלערב הו אלתקדיר וקד יסתעמלונה פי אפעאל אלמחדתׄין כקולהם כׄלק אלכׄיאט אלקמיץ אדׄא קדרה ויקול פי אלעבראני מי יצר אל (ישעיה מד:י). ויקרב אן מעני דׄלך פי אללגתין מתקארב ולשון בריאה משהורה̈ יכׄתץ בה סבחאנה. פאמא מא יסתעמל מן מתׄאל דׄלך פי בני אדם כקו׳ ובראת לך שם (יהושע יז:טו) ויד ברא (יחזקאל כא:כד) פאנה מע תסאוי אלחרף פי אלגׄמיע יפסר מן אלתנקיה̈ ואלתמייז ויכון להדׄה אללגׄה̈ עלי הדׄא אלקול אקסאם א׳ מא אצלה אלבא ואלריש פקט מע אכׄתלאף תצריפה כקו׳ ולבור את כל זה (קהלת ט:א). וברותי מכם (יחזקאל כ:לח). הברו נשאי כלי ייי (ישעיהו נב:יא). ותׄאניהא מא ינצׄאף אלי הדׄה אלחרפין הא אצליה̈ איצׄא כקו׳ הברי שמים (ישעיהו מז:יג). ותׄאלתׄהא מא יתראדף פיה אלריש כקו׳ ברור מללו (איוב לג:ג). וד מא אצלה אלאלף מצׄאפה̈ אלי אלבא ואלריש חסב מא תקדם מן ברא וגירה.
content.english: "And his saying ‘created’" (bara). He glosses [the verb] as "created"¹ in the sense of "formed"² — as in his words va-yivra Elohim et ha-Adam "And God created the man" (Gen 1:27) and va-yiṣer YHWH Elohim et ha-Adam "And the LORD God formed the man" (Gen 2:7). Now the Hebrew form³ yetzirah is shared between the Eternal (mighty and majestic) and creaturely [agents] — as in His words of Him, Yoṣer ha-Areṣ ve-ʿOseh "He who forms the earth and makes it" (Isa 45:18), and of them, Yoṣrey fesel kullam "all the makers of an idol" (Isa 44:9). But [in such cases] when [the verb] is interpreted of Him (may He be exalted), it is from the meaning of "creation"¹, and when of them, it is from the meaning of "shaping"⁴ — so as to remove ambiguity. For the basic meaning⁵ of khalq in the language of the Arabs is "proportioning"⁶, and they sometimes apply it to creaturely acts — as in their saying khalaqa al-khayyāṭ al-qamīṣa "the tailor designed the shirt," when he measured it out. And in Hebrew it is said Mi yaṣar el? "Who has formed a god?" (Isa 44:10). It is plausible⁷ that the meaning [of this root] in the two languages is closely matched. The Hebrew form beriʾah is renowned: it is reserved⁸ for Him (praise be to Him). As for instances where the same [root b-r-ʾ] is used of human beings — as in u-vareta lekha sham "and cut out for yourself there" (Josh 17:15) and yad bāra "a hand of cutting" (Ezek 21:24) — [in those cases,] although the consonants are identical in all instances, [the meaning] is to be interpreted from [the senses of] "clarifying"⁹ and "distinguishing"¹⁰. On this account, this Hebrew form may be sorted into the following categories¹¹: first, those whose root is just the bā and resh, with various conjugations — as in u-le-vor et kol zeh "and to investigate all this" (Eccl 9:1), u-varotī mi-kem "I will purge from among you" (Ezek 20:38), and hibbarū nosʾei kelei YHWH "be pure, you who bear the LORD's vessels" (Isa 52:11). Second, those to which a he is added (treated as a root letter¹²) — as in hovrei shamayim "the diviners of the heavens" (Isa 47:13). Third, those in which the resh is reduplicated — as in bārur millō "his speech was clear" (Job 33:3). And fourth, those whose [first] root letter is an aleph adjoined to the bā and resh — as in bara itself and the like.
content.comments: ¹ khalq (خلق) — Arabic "creation"; here used as the gloss for Hebrew bara. ² yaṣara (يصر) — Ali's Arabic rendering for Hebrew yāṣar (יצר); see also taṣwīr. ³ lashon (לשון) — Hebrew technical term for "verbal form / linguistic category." Karaite J-A authors regularly preserve lashon unchanged when discussing Hebrew morphology. ⁴ taṣwīr (تصوير) — "shaping, giving form to," Ali's gloss for the creaturely sense of y-ṣ-r distinct from the divine sense of khalq. ⁵ aṣl (أصل) — "root, basic [lexical] meaning"; one of the most polysemous terms in Karaite usage (also: derivational base; theological principle). ⁶ See glossary s.v. taqdīr. ⁷ yaqrub (يقرب) — "it is plausible"; pairs with yabʿud / baʿīd. ⁸ yakhtaṣṣu bihi (يختصّ به) — "is reserved to Him alone"; technical formula for divine-exclusive vocabulary. ⁹ tanqiya (تنقية) — "clarifying, purifying," applied to the human-creaturely sense of b-r-ʾ in Eccl 9:1 etc. ¹⁰ tamyīz (تمييز) — "distinguishing"; in formal nahw, "specifier" (a syntactic category), but here in its base sense of "drawing distinctions." ¹¹ aqsām (أقسام) — "categories, divisions"; sing. qism. Standard term for analytical partition. ¹² ʾaṣliyya (أصلية) — "[treated as] a root letter"; cf. mabnī / murakkab for affixed letters.

content.hebrew: וקו׳ אלהים – הדׄא אלאסם מן גׄמלה̈ אסמא[ה] תע׳ יפיד אסתחקאק אלעבאדה̈ כקו׳ והיה ייי לי לאלהים (בראשית כח:כא) אהיה לאלהים לכל משפחות (ירמיהו לא:א). ולדׄלך למא אעתקד אלמכׄאלפין פי אלותׄן אנה יסתחק אלעבאדה̈ אסמוה בדׄלך כקו׳ את אלהי אשר עשיתי לקחתם (שופטים יח:כד). קום עשה
content.english: "And his saying ‘God’" (Elohim). This name is one of His names (may He be exalted) and it conveys deserving-of-worship¹ — as in His words ve-hayah YHWH lī le-Elohim "and the LORD shall be unto me for a God" (Gen 28:21), Ehyeh le-Elohim le-khol mishpeḥot "I shall be God to all the families" (Jer 31:1). And for this reason, when the dissenters concerning the idol² came to believe that it deserves worship, they called it by this [name] — as in et Elohai asher ʿasiti leqaḥtem "you have taken the gods that I made" (Judg 18:24); "Arise, make...
content.comments: ¹ istiḥqāq al-ʿibāda (استحقاق العبادة) — "deserving of worship"; a kalām-philosophical phrase used to define the semantic content of the divine name. ² al-mukhālifīn fī al-wathan (المخالفين في الوثن) — "those who depart [from monotheism] regarding the idol"; al-mukhālifīn elsewhere often = Rabbanites, but here clearly refers to the idolaters of Judg 18 (Micah's idol).

content.hebrew: לנו אלהים (שמות לב:א). פקד אקתצׄי הדׄא אלאסם וגיר מן תסתחק עליה עבאדתה עז וגׄל. והדׄא ממא יוכד כׄלק אלמלאיכה̈ קבל כׄלק אלעאלם או מעה ליסתחק עליהם אלעבאדה̈ אדׄ קבל כׄלק אלעאבד לא יחסן תסמיתה מעבודא כמא לא יחסן עלי אלתחקיק תסמיה̈ אלמצׄרוב מצׄרובא וצׄארב ליס.
content.english: … lanu Elohim "for us a god" (Exod 32:1)." So this name [Elohim] has been made to entail [the deserving-of-worship of] one other than Him to whom worship is rightly due (mighty and majestic). And this is among the [considerations] that support [the view] that the angels were created before the world or together with it — so that worship might be due from them: for prior to the creation of the worshipper, the worshipped cannot properly be named "worshipped" — just as, strictly speaking, one who is to be struck cannot be named "struck" when there is [as yet] no one to strike him.

content.hebrew: וקו׳ את – הי לפטׄה̈ ת[ס]מי פי אלערבי חרפא תדכׄל עלי אלמפעול פתמיזה מן פאעלה ולדׄלך ענד ארתפאעהא ילתבסאן נחו אבנים שחקו מים (ישעיה יד:יט).
content.english: "And his saying ‘et’" (et). This is a word called in Arabic [grammar] a particle¹: it precedes the object² and thereby distinguishes it from its subject³ — and for this reason, when it is omitted, the two [roles] become indistinguishable, as in avanim shaḥaqu mayim — "stones — waters wear them down" [or, equally, "waters — stones wear them down"] (Isa 14:19).
content.comments: ¹ ḥarf (حرف) — the Arabic grammatical category subsuming both "particle" and "letter"; here, the "particle" sense, specifically the object-marking ḥarf nominative for the Hebrew et. ² mafʿūl (مفعول) — grammatical object. Abū l-Faraj distinguishes five subtypes (muṭlaq, bihi, fīhi, lahu, maʿahu); the present is mafʿūl bihi, the direct object. ³ fāʿil (فاعل) — grammatical subject / agent of the verb.

content.hebrew: – וקו׳ השמים ואת הארץ – הו אשארה̈ אלי מערוף מעהוד פלדׄלך חסן דכׄול הא אלתעריף עליהמא אבתדאא מן גיר תקדם דׄכרהמא נכרה̈ מתׄל והיה האיש ההוא (איוב א:ב) אלדׄי דכׄלת עליה הא אלתעריף בעד תקדם דׄכרה נכרה כקו׳ איש היה בארץ עוץ (איוב א:א). פלמא כאנת אלסמא אלעליא מעלומה̈ באלכׄבר ואלארץׄ באלחס אורדהמא בהא אלתעריף מן גיר תנכיר מתקדם ולא נעת מתאכׄר מתל והיה האיש אשר יבחר ייי (במדבר טז:ז) ולא יקתצׄי תקדים דׄכר אלסמא עלי אלארץׄ כונהא מכׄלוקה̈ קבלהא אדׄ ואו אלעטף אלתי פי ואת הארץ לא תפיד דׄלך בל יגׄוז כׄלקהמא מעא ויגׄוז תקדם כׄלק אחדאהמא לכׄלק אלאכׄרי לכן אלאקרב כׄלקהמא וקתא ואחדא עלי מא תקדם מן תפסיר בראשית מע אול מכׄלוק או בעד אול מכׄלוק מן חיתׄ אן אלארץׄ כׄלקת מתאכׄרה̈ ען אלסמא למא כאנת מכׄלוקה̈ מע אול מכׄלוק ולא בעדה בל אלסמא פקט בדׄלך אחק ולעלה תע׳ קצד בתקדים דׄכר אלארץׄ עלי אלסמא פי מוצׄע אכׄר כקו׳ ביום עשות ייי אלהים ארץ ושמים (בראשית ב:ד) רפע שבהה̈ עמן יתוהם דׄלך. ואנמא יקדם דׄכר אלסמא עלי אלארץׄ פי כתׄי[ר] מן אלמואצׄע לכׄצוציתהא ען אלארץׄ באמור כתׄירה̈ אחדהא כונהא כרסיא לוקארה כקו׳ השמים כסאי (ישעיה סו:א).
content.english: "And his saying ‘the heavens and the earth’" (ha-shamayim ve-et ha-areṣ). This is a reference¹ to something familiar and well-known [to the reader], and that is why it is appropriate for the ha of definiteness² (the Hebrew definite article) to enter upon them at the outset, without their having been previously mentioned in the indefinite³ — unlike ve-hayah ha-ʾish ha-hu "and that man shall be" (Job 1:2), where the ha of definiteness enters after the man has been previously mentioned in the indefinite, as in ʾish hayah be-ereṣ Uṣ "there was a man in the land of Uz" (Job 1:1). So because the upper heavens are known by [traditional] report⁴ and the earth by the senses⁵, [Scripture] brings them in with the ha of definiteness, without any prior indefinite mention and without any subsequent attribute⁶ — unlike ve-hayah ha-ʾish asher yivḥar YHWH "and the man whom the LORD chooses shall be" (Num 16:7). [Scripture's] mentioning the heavens before the earth does not entail that they were created before [the earth], since the vāv of conjunction⁷ in ve-et ha-areṣ does not convey that; rather, [it] permits that they were created together or that the creation of one preceded the creation of the other. But the most plausible view is that they were created at a single time, on the preceding interpretation of bereshit [as "together with the first thing created" or "after the first thing created"]; for the earth was created [as] late [as] the heavens [were], being created together with the first created thing and not after it — yet the heavens alone are most worthy in this respect [of being mentioned first]. And perhaps He, may He be exalted, intended in another place — as in be-yom ʿasot YHWH Elohim ereṣ ve-shamayim "in the day the LORD God made earth and heavens" (Gen 2:4) — by putting the mention of the earth before the heavens, to remove the [potential] doubt of one who might imagine [that the heavens preceded the earth]. And He puts the mention of the heavens before the earth in many places because of their being distinguished from the earth by many things — one of which is their being a throne for His glory, as in ha-shamayim kisʾī "the heavens are my throne" (Isa 66:1).
content.comments: ¹ ishāra (إشارة) — "reference / indication"; semantically a deictic pointing to a known referent. ² hāʾ al-taʿrīf (هاء التعريف) — lit. "the ה of definiteness," Ali's Arabic name for the Hebrew definite article ה (the prefix ה- of הַשָּׁמַיִם, etc.). He maps it onto the Arabic ال. ³ tankīr / nakira (تنكير / نكرة) — "indefiniteness" / "indefinite noun"; pairs with taʿrīf / maʿrifa. ⁴ al-khabar (الخبر) — "[traditional] report," knowledge by transmission. Pairs with al-ḥiss as the two ways of knowing. ⁵ al-ḥiss (الحسّ) — "the senses," empirical knowledge. ⁶ naʿt (نعت) — "attribute, qualifying modifier"; here, a restrictive relative clause that would otherwise definitize a preceding indefinite noun. ⁷ vāv of conjunction (واو العطف, wāw al-ʿaṭf) — Ali's name for the conjunctive ו, mapped onto the Arabic wāw al-ʿaṭf. ʿaṭf = "conjunction."

content.hebrew: Gen 1:2
content.english: Gen 1:2

content.hebrew: והארץ היתה – וג׳ – קו׳ והארץ לם יתקדם מא תכון אלואו פיהא עטפא עליה ואלאקרב כונהא ואו אלאבתדי מתׄל אלואואת אלדאכׄלה̈ עלי אלאכׄבאר אלמבתדאה̈ נחו ואברהם זקן (בראשית כד:א). ונח מצא חן (בראשית ו:ח).
content.english: "And the earth was" (ve-ha-areṣ hayetah). His words "and the earth": nothing has preceded for the vāv [in it] to function as a vāv of conjunction¹ with. The most plausible is that it is the vāv of opening², like the vāvs that enter upon predicates that begin [new propositions]³, as in ve-Avraham zaqen "And Abraham was old" (Gen 24:1) and ve-Noaḥ maṣa ḥen "And Noah found favor" (Gen 6:8).
content.comments: ¹ wāw al-ʿaṭf (واو العطف) — "vāv of conjunction"; cf. seg. 30 above. The conjunctive ו linking to a prior antecedent. ² wāw al-ibtidāʾ (واو الابتداء) — "vāv of opening / inception"; the ו prefixed to the first word of a new, independent narrative clause, with no syntactic dependence on what precedes. Karaite calque on the Arabic grammarians' wāw al-istiʾnāf / wāw al-ibtidāʾ. ³ al-akhbār al-mubtadaʾa (الأخبار المبتدأة) — "the [propositional] reports that begin [a new discourse]"; opening clauses introducing new narrative units. khabar here in its broader sense of "report / declarative clause," not the strict syntactic "predicate."

content.hebrew: – וקו׳ תהו ובהו – האתאן אללפטׄאן ליסתא ממא יתצרף ולא ישתהר וגׄודה ואלאקרב אן פאידתהמא אלכׄלו מן אלחיואן ואלעמראן כקו׳ פי כׄראב ארץ אדום עלי טריק אלתשביה ונטה עליה קו תהו ואבני בהו (ישעיהו לד:יא) וקו׳ לא תהו בראה לשבת יצרה (ישעיהו מה:יח). פאורא תע׳ אן תהו ובהו באלצׄד ללסכנא
content.english: "tohu va-vohu" (tohu va-vohu). These two words are not among [the words] that inflect¹, nor is their occurrence widely attested. The most plausible is that their import² is emptiness of living being and habitation, as in his words concerning the desolation of the land of Edom — by way of comparison³ — and-He-shall-stretch over it "a line of tohu and stones of bohu" (Isa 34:11), and his words "He did not create it tohu, He formed it to be inhabited" (Isa 45:18). So he indicated⁴ (may He be exalted) that tohu and vohu are the contrary of habitation.
content.comments: ¹ yataṣarrafu (يتصرف) — "inflects [verbally]"; from taṣarruf, "inflection." The point is that these are frozen lexical items with no verbal paradigm. ² fāʾida (فائدة) — "import, semantic yield"; the meaning that a word or construction conveys. ³ ʿalā ṭarīq al-tashbīh (على طريق التشبيه) — "by way of comparison / simile"; the desolation of Edom is likened to primordial tohu va-vohu, not literally identified with it. ⁴ awrā (أورى) — "he indicated, made manifest"; the act of bringing a meaning to light by allusion.

content.hebrew: וקאל ראיתי את הארץ והנה תהו ובהו (ירמיהו ד:כג) בעד מא קאל מא הו כאלשרח לה מן קו׳ ראיתי ההרים וג׳ (ירמיהו ד:כד) ראיתי והנה אין האדם וג׳ (ירמיהו ד:כה) ראיתי והנה הכרמל וג׳ (ירמיהו ד:כו) פאתצׄח מן מגׄמוע דׄלך אן פאידתהמא מא תקדם דׄכרה והמא בוזן בחן (ישעיהו כח:טז) בהן (שמות כט:כ) ואנמא לם יגי אכׄרהמא מפתוחא מתׄלהמא לאגׄל אלואו אלתי מן שאנהא אלצׄם.
content.english: And he said "I looked at the earth, and behold, it was tohu va-vohu" (Jer 4:23) after he had said what serves as an explanation for it from his words "I looked at the mountains..." (Jer 4:24), "I looked, and behold there was no man..." (Jer 4:25), "I looked, and behold the [fruitful land = ha-]Karmel..." (Jer 4:26). It becomes clear from the sum of this that their import is what has been mentioned beforehand. And the two are on the pattern¹ of boḥan (Isa 28:16) [and] bohen (Exod 29:20); the only reason that the final [letter] of the two does not come with the [vowel] patah² like those is on account of the vāv, whose nature is to require the [vowel] ḍamma³.
content.comments: ¹ bi-wazn (بوزن) — "on the [morphological] pattern of"; cf. seg. 23 above (Gen 1:1 bara). Ali invokes the Karaite paqāl-class words ending in -n to which tohu and bohu would belong but for the holam vowel. ² maftūḥan (مفتوحا) — "[vocalized] with the patah"; Ali maps the Hebrew patah to the Arabic fatḥa, the a-class vowel. ³ al-ḍamma (الضمة) — "the [vowel] ḍamma"; the u-class vowel. Ali identifies the Hebrew holam/shureq with Arabic ḍamma. The argument: -u-ending forces the prior consonant's vowel to align with it, displacing the expected a.

content.hebrew: וקו׳ וחשך – קיל אנה סואד יחל פי אלהוא אלדׄי קאל ענה ורוח אלהים (בראשית א:ב) פיחצל אלטׄלאם מנה. וקיל בל הו אגׄזא סוד מתכאתפה̈ פי בעץׄ אלגׄהאת כקולה הבאת אל אצרות חשך וג׳ (איוב לח:כב) פינקלה תע׳ אלי אלמוצׄע אלדׄי יריד כון אלחשך פיה חסב מא פעל פי מצרים כקו׳ ויהי חשך אפלה בכל ארץ מצרים (שמות י:כב). ויגׄוז כלא אלקולאן ויטאבקהמא תשת חשך ויהי לילה (תהלים קא:כ) פאמא מן זעם אנה ליס בשי חאדתׄ בל הו זואל אלנור פבעיד למא תקדם ולקו׳ יוצר אור וב׳ חש׳ (ישעיה מה:ז) פיגׄוז כון
content.english: "and darkness" (ve-ḥoshekh). Some have said that it is a blackness that subsists in the air of which he spoke ve-ruaḥ Elohim "and the spirit of God" (Gen 1:2), and the dimness comes about from it. And some have said: rather, it is dark particles compressed in certain quarters, as in his words "Have you entered the storehouses of darkness..." (Job 38:22); so He (may He be exalted) transfers them to the place in which He wills darkness to occur, in accordance with what He did in Egypt, as in his words "And there was thick darkness in all the land of Egypt" (Exod 10:22). Both views are admissible¹, and what corresponds to them is "You make darkness and it is night" (Ps 104:20). As for one who claims that it is not an originated thing² but rather the privation of light³ — that is far-fetched, by what has preceded, and by his words "[He who] forms light and creates darkness" (Isa 45:7). For it is admissible that...
content.comments: ¹ yajūzu (يجوز) — "it is admissible"; cf. yajūz / jāʾiz, the standard Karaite category for an interpretively permissible reading (without being the al-aqrab). ² shayʾ ḥādith (شيء حادث) — "an originated [created] thing," something that has come into being. Pairs with qadīm (eternal) in kalām. ³ zawāl al-nūr (زوال النور) — "the privation [lit. departure] of light"; the privative-theory of darkness, which Ali rejects as inconsistent with darkness being something God creates (Isa 45:7) and stores up (Job 38:22).

content.hebrew: אלאול אגׄזא ביץׄ צאפיה̈ ינקלהא תע׳ או ביאץׄ יחל פי אלהוא פינתפי בה אלסואד אלדׄי כאן חשך.
content.english: ...the first [view be that they are] white pure particles which He (may He be exalted) transfers, or [that it is] a whiteness that subsists in the air, whereby the blackness which was "darkness" is negated.

content.hebrew: – וקו׳ על פני תהום – אפאד כונה עלי טׄאהר אלמא והדׄה אללפטׄה̈ תנבי ען אלמיאה ילגׄוזיה̈ כקו׳ כל מעינות תהום רבה (בראשית ז:יא) את תהום וכסוך המים הרבים (יחזקאל כו:יט). תהום אמר לא [בי][1] היא (איוב כח:יד). ואשבאה דׄלך.
content.english: "upon the face of the deep" (ʿal pene tehom). He conveyed [that] He [was] upon the surface of the water; and this word [tehom] gives notice of abundant waters¹, as in his words "all the springs of the great tehom" (Gen 7:11), "the tehom and the abundant waters [that] cover you" (Ezek 26:19), "tehom said: it is not [in me]…" (Job 28:14), and [other phrases] of the same kind.
content.comments: ¹ al-miyāh al-ghazīra (المياه الغزيرة) — "abundant / copious waters," the reading I have adopted for the JA ms.'s ילגׄוזיה̈. The form as written is orthographically irregular; the proposed reading (with mis-segmentation of an initial al-) fits the semantic context — the cited proof-texts all stress the deep's vastness (rabbah, ha-rabbim). An alternative reading would take it as a corruption of al-lujjiyya (اللجّية), "abyssal"; the sense is similar.

content.hebrew: ורוח אלהים מרחפת – וג׳ – יעני תחרך אלהוא אלמתצׄמן אלחשך עלי אלקולין אלמתקדמין ואצׄאף
content.english: "And the spirit of God hovered" (ve-ruaḥ Elohim meraḥefet, etc.). He means: the movement of the air containing the darkness, on the two preceding views. And he ascribed...

content.hebrew: אלרוח אליה תע׳ דון אלחשך ואלרוח למא כאנת לה כאלאלה̈ פי אפעאל כתׄירה̈ כקו׳ ישב רוחו יזלו מים (תהלים קמז:יח). הגה ברוחו הקשה (ישעיהו כז:ח). רוח סערה עשה דברו (תהלים קמח:ח). ברוח קדים תשבר אניות (תהלים מח:ח). וגיר דׄלך ממא ינסב תאתׄיר אלפעל פיה אלי אלרוח לכונהא סבבא לה מע אסתגנאיה עז וגׄל פי אפעאלה ען דׄלך לכנה יפעלה למצאלח אלמכלפין חסב מא גׄרת בה אלעאדה̈.
content.english: ...the wind to Him (may He be exalted), and not the darkness — since the wind, given that it functions for Him as if an instrument¹ in many acts (as in his words "He makes his wind blow, the waters flow" (Ps 147:18); "He removed [them] with his harsh blast" (Isa 27:8); "stormy wind fulfilling his word" (Ps 148:8); "with the east wind you shatter the ships [of Tarshish]" (Ps 48:8); and other [verses] in which the effecting of the act is attributed to the wind by its being a cause² for it — even though He (mighty and majestic) is independent³ in His acts of [needing] that, but does this for the benefits of the obligated⁴, in accordance with what has come to be customary⁵).
content.comments: ¹ ka-l-āla (كالآلة) — "as if an instrument"; technical kalām designation for the secondary cause through which divine action is mediated. The "as if" preserves the doctrine that God is independent of instruments yet acts through them by way of accommodation. ² sabab (سبب) — "cause"; here the proximate cause, not the agent-cause. Pairs with musabbib (Causer = God). ³ istighnāʾ (استغناء) — "independence, self-sufficiency"; the divine attribute of being free from any need. ⁴ al-mukallafīn (المكلّفين) — "the [morally] obligated"; the standard Muʿtazilite designation for the class of rational creatures upon whom religious obligation falls. ⁵ jarat bi-hi al-ʿāda (جرت به العادة) — "it has become customary"; standard kalām formula for God's regular mode of operation through secondary causes (ʿāda).

content.hebrew: Gen 1:3
content.english: Gen 1:3

content.hebrew: ויאמר אלהים – יקאל אנה אחדתׄ כלאמא הו יהי אור (בראשית א:ג). סמעתה אלמלאיכה̈ ופהמתה ואנצלחת באכׄבארה עז וגׄל להא בדׄלך ועלמת אנה סיכון אסתדלאלא תׄם אצׄטרת אלי אלעלם באלאור
content.english: "And God said" (va-yomer Elohim). It is said that He originated¹ speech, namely yehi or "Let there be light" (Gen 1:3). The angels heard it and understood it, and were made [thereby] fit by His informing them (mighty and majestic) of this; and they knew that it would come to be — [knowing this first] by inference², then they were compelled³ to knowledge of the light...
content.comments: ¹ aḥdatha (أحدث) — "He originated, brought into being"; from ḥadath / iḥdāth, the kalām verb for the creation of an originated entity (ḥādith) as opposed to the eternal (qadīm). Here applied to divine speech — a created act of speech, on the standard Muʿtazilite doctrine that God's speech is created. ² istidlālan (استدلالا) — "by way of inference / demonstrative reasoning"; the angels' knowledge of the light's coming-to-be is acquired by the rational inference from God's announcement, prior to its actual occurrence. ³ uḍṭurrat ilā al-ʿilm (اضطرت إلى العلم) — "they were compelled to knowledge"; here, ʿilm ḍarūrī, "necessary [immediate] knowledge," as opposed to ʿilm muktasab / istidlālī, "acquired / inferential knowledge." The contrast is canonical kalām epistemology.

content.hebrew: למא חדתׄ. ולא יחסן מנה עז וגׄל הדׄא אלכלאם אלאבעד אן חצל מן בעצׄהם מע בעץׄ מואצׄעה עלי קדר מן אלכׄטאב פהמו מעה דׄלך. וקיל אן מעני ויאמר אראד מתׄל מה תאמר נפשך (שמואל א׳ כ:ד).
content.english: ...when it came to be. And this speech would not be appropriate¹ on His part (mighty and majestic) unless it had come about that they [the angels] had reached among themselves a convention² regarding some measure of address, by which they would [be able to] understand it. And it has been said that the meaning of va-yomer means "he willed," like "whatever your soul says [= desires]" (1 Sam 20:4).
content.comments: ¹ lā yaḥsunu (لا يحسن) — "it would not be fitting / appropriate"; standard Muʿtazilite ethical category. Pairs with qabīḥ (reprehensible). ² muwāḍaʿa (مواضعة) — "[linguistic] convention"; the Muʿtazilite-Karaite doctrine that signifier-signified relations are established by agreement (rather than by divine institution or natural correspondence). The argument here is that even God's address to the angels presupposes a prior conventional language among them.

content.hebrew: – וקו׳ יהי – מענאה יחדתׄ אדׄ לשון היות אדׄא תנאול אלאסם דון כׄברה אפאד אלחדתׄ כקו׳ יהי אור (בראשית א:ג) יהי רקיע (בראשית א:ו) יהי מאורות (בראשית א:יד) ואשבאה דׄלך. וקו׳ יכון לה כׄבר אדׄא לם
content.english: "Let there be" (yehi). Its meaning is "let it come into being"¹, since the [Hebrew] verbal-form² hāyot, when it takes the [subject] noun without its predicate³, conveys coming-into-being, as in his words yehi or "Let there be light" (Gen 1:3), yehi raqiyaʿ "Let there be a firmament" (Gen 1:6), yehi meʾorot "Let there be luminaries" (Gen 1:14), and the like. And [this verb] takes a predicate when it does not come...
content.comments: ¹ yaḥduthu (يحدث) — "let it come into being"; the verbal counterpart of aḥdatha (cf. seg. 44 above). Ali draws a sharp lexical distinction within Hebrew ה.י.ה between the absolute / existential sense (= "come into being") and the copular sense. ² lashon (לשון) — Hebrew technical term for "verbal form / linguistic category"; cf. seg. 23 above. ³ ism / khabar (اسم / خبر) — "subject / predicate"; the standard Arabic nominal-clause analysis. Ali applies it to Hebrew: when ה.י.ה takes only an ism, it is existential; when it takes both ism and khabar, it is copular.

content.hebrew: יגׄי כדׄלך נחו יהי ייי אלהיך ברוך (מלכים א׳ י:ט). יהיה ייי אחד (זכריה יד:ט). ומא יגׄרי מגׄראהמא מן לשון היות אלתי לה אסם וכׄבר פייי תע׳ הו אלאסם ואלכׄבר ברוך ואחד וכדׄלך פי אלערבי להא אסם וכׄבר כקולך
content.english: ...in this manner¹, as in yehi YHWH Elohekha barukh "Blessed be the LORD your God" (1 Kgs 10:9), yihyeh YHWH eḥad "The LORD shall be one" (Zech 14:9), and whatever runs the course of these² of [the instances of] the verbal-form hāyot which has [both] a subject and a predicate. So "the LORD" (may He be exalted) is the subject, and "blessed" and "one" are the predicates. And likewise in Arabic [the corresponding verb kāna] has a subject and a predicate, as when you say...
content.comments: ¹ yajīʾu kadhālika (يجيء كذلك) — "it comes in this manner"; the construction without a predicate (i.e., the existential / creative sense). ² See glossary s.v. yajrī majrā.

content.hebrew: כאן זיד דׄאהבא.
content.english: ...kāna Zayd dhāhiban ["Zayd was going"].

content.hebrew: – וקו׳ אור – קיל אנה גׄסם צׄוי ינבת ענה אלנור וינפדׄ אלשעאע גׄאר מגׄרי אלשמס ואנה כׄלק פי גׄהה̈ אלשרק לילא תׄם טׄהר גדאה̈ יום אלאחד ואשרק נורה עלי אלעאלם וסאר פי אלסמא כמסיר אלשמס אלי אן גאב בעד
content.english: "light" (or). It has been said that it is a luminous body¹ from which light grows forth and rays emanate, running the course of the sun²; and that it was created in the eastern region at night, then appeared on the morning of Sunday, and its light shone upon the world, and it moved through the heavens like the movement of the sun, until it set after...
content.comments: ¹ jism ḍawʾī (جسم ضوئي) — "luminous body"; the substrate-theory of light as a physical body bearing the accident of luminance, as opposed to light as a non-bodily accident or a privation. The contrast continues the realist program of seg. 36 (against darkness as privation). ² jārin majrā al-shams (جار مجرى الشمس) — "running the course of the sun"; Karaite signature formula for analogical class-membership, here cosmological: the primordial light behaves on the pattern of the sun's diurnal motion.

content.hebrew: אלמסא וסאר באלליל תחת אלארץׄ אלי אן טׄהר גדאה̈ אליו[ם] אלתׄאני וכדׄלך גׄרת חאלה פי אלג׳ איאם ואנה פי אליום אלדׄ למא קאל סבחאנה יהי מאורות (בראשית י:יד) תפצל אלי אן צאר מנה אלשמס ואלקמר ואלכואכב. וימכן אן יקאל עכס מא קיל פי אלחשך.
content.english: ...evening, and [then] it traveled at night beneath the earth until it appeared on the morning of the second day. So its state proceeded in like manner over [the first] three days. Then on the fourth day, when He (praise be to Him) said yehi meʾorot "Let there be luminaries" (Gen 1:14)¹, it [the primordial light] was apportioned² so that from it there came the sun, the moon, and the stars. And it is possible to say [of light] the inverse of what was said concerning darkness.
content.comments: ¹ The JA citation as transmitted gives בראשית י:יד; the actual referent is Gen 1:14 (yehi meʾorot). Almost certainly a scribal slip in the transmission, the א of the chapter-number having dropped. ² tafaḍḍala (تفضّل) — "it was apportioned / divided out"; from f-ḍ-l. The primordial light is partitioned among the luminaries of day four.

content.hebrew: Gen 1:4
content.english: Gen 1:4

content.hebrew: וירא אלהים את האור – וג׳ – אלראיה פי הדׄא אלמוצׄע במעני אלעלם אמארה דׄלך תעדיהא אלי
content.english: "And God saw the light" (va-yarʾ Elohim et ha-or, etc.). "Seeing" in this place is in the sense of "knowing."¹ The sign² of this is that it [the verb] takes two...
content.comments: ¹ ʿilm (علم) — "knowledge"; here, the cognitive (rather than perceptual) sense of the verb r-ʾ-h. ² amāra (أمارة) — "sign, indicator"; the diagnostic feature by which one identifies a particular semantic value of a polysemous form.

content.hebrew: מפעולין והמא אור טוב מן חיתׄ אנהא אדׄא אפאדת רויה̈ אלעין תעדת אלי מפעול ואחד כקו׳ וירא יוסף
content.english: ...objects¹, namely "the light" and "good"² — since [the verb], whenever it conveys the eye's sight, takes [only] one object³, as in "And Joseph saw...
content.comments: ¹ mafʿūlīn (مفعولين) — "[two] objects"; here the dual of mafʿūl bihi (direct object). Ali invokes the canonical Karaite criterion that the cognitive sense of r-ʾ-y is doubly transitive while the perceptual sense is singly transitive. ² ūr ṭov (אור טוב) — Ali analyses the Hebrew as "saw the light [to be] good," with ṭov a predicative second object. ³ mafʿūl wāḥid (مفعول واحد) — "one [direct] object."

content.hebrew: את אחיו (בראשית מב:ז) ואמתׄאל דׄלך והדׄא חכם אלרויה̈ פי לגה̈ אלערב כקולהם ראית זיד פאצׄלא יענון עלמתה פאצׄלא פלדׄלך קלת אן מעני האדׄא אלראיה עלם אלאלאה אלנור גׄידא וליס הדׄא אלקול פיה תע׳ לכונה גיר ראי בחאסה פיכון גׄמיע מא יטלק עליה מן לפטׄ ראיה יפיד אלעלם בל הו פיה עז וגׄל ופי אלמכׄלוקין עלי סוא לאן לה בכונה מדרכא צפה̈ זאידה̈ עלי כונה עאלמא פהו סבחאנה ירי אלמראיאת ויסמע אלמסמועאת לכונה חיא אלאפאת ענה מרתפעה̈ ויעלמהא לכונה עאלמא לנפסה פאדׄא קאל וירא אלהים את בני ישראל (שמות ב:כה). וישמע אלהים את נאקתם (בראשית ב:כד) פדׄלך יפיד אלרויה̈ ואלסאמע תחקיקא.
content.english: ...his brothers" (Gen 42:7) and the like. And this is the rule¹ of [the verb of] seeing in the language of the Arabs as well — as in their saying raʾaytu Zayd faḍilan "I saw Zayd [as] excellent," by which they mean ʿalimtuhu faḍilan "I knew him [to be] excellent." For this reason I have said that the meaning of this [verb of] seeing [here] is that God knew the light [to be] good. This statement does not [hold] of Him (may He be exalted) by reason of His not being one who perceives by a [sensory] faculty — so that every term that may be applied to Him expressing "sight" would [merely] convey knowing. Rather, [the case] is with Him (mighty and majestic) and with creatures on a par²: for in His being one who perceives there is a superadded attribute³ over and above His being one who knows. Thus He (praise be to Him) sees the [things] visible and hears the [things] audible by virtue of His being living — defects⁴ being lifted away from Him — and He knows them by virtue of His being one who knows in Himself. So when He says "And God saw the children of Israel" (Exod 2:25) and "And God heard their groaning" (Exod 2:24), that conveys [actual] seeing and hearing in truth⁵.
content.comments: ¹ ḥukm (حكم) — "rule, regulation"; the regular syntactic/semantic behavior of a lexeme. ² ʿalā sawāʾ (على سواء) — "on a par, equally"; signals the kalām thesis that the divine and human attributes of perception are predicated univocally (with the qualification of His freedom from defect). ³ ṣifa zāʾida (صفة زائدة) — "a superadded attribute"; standard Muʿtazilite terminology for an attribute that exceeds the bare attribute of essence. ⁴ āfāt (آفات) — "defects, impairments"; the bodily limitations of which God is free. ⁵ taḥqīqan (تحقيقا) — "in truth, actually"; the predication holds in its full literal force, not figuratively (majāz).

content.hebrew: – וקו׳ כי טוב – יעני עלמה גׄידא נאפעא ללמכׄלוקין כקו׳ ומתוק האור וטוב לע׳ (קהלת יא:ז) וליס עלמה עז וגׄל בהדׄה אלצפה̈ בעד כׄלקה איאה בל הו עאלם בדׄלך מן חאלה מן קבל ומן בעד.
content.english: "that it was good" (ki ṭov). [That is,] He knew it [to be] good [and] beneficial to the creatures, as in His words u-matoq ha-or ve-ṭov la-ʿeinayim "and sweet is the light, and good for the eyes" (Eccl 11:7). And this is not [some] knowledge of His (mighty and majestic) acquired by this attribute after His creating it; rather, He is one who knows this from His [eternal] state, prior and posterior¹.
content.comments: ¹ min ḥālihi min qabl wa-min baʿd (من حاله من قبل ومن بعد) — "from His state, before and after"; the divine knowledge is non-temporal, not contingent upon the act of creation. Standard Muʿtazilite formula against the proposition that God acquires new knowledge through new acts.

content.hebrew: – וקולה ויבדל אלהים בין האור ובין החשך – מענאה פצל בין זמאן אלנור ובין זמאן אלטׄלמה̈ והדׄא אלפצל ירגׄע אלי אנה ענד וגׄוד אלאור ירתפע אלחשך וענד חצול אלחשך יזול אלאור אמא בנקל אלאגׄזא אלביץׄ
content.english: "And God separated between the light and between the darkness" (va-yavdel Elohim bein ha-or u-vein ha-ḥoshekh). Its meaning is: He separated between the time of light and the time of darkness; and this separation comes down to [the fact] that upon the existence of the light, the darkness is lifted away, and upon the obtaining of the darkness, the light passes away — either by the transferring of the bright, pure particles...

content.hebrew: אלצאפיה̈ אלי בעץׄ אלגׄהאת וגׄעל אלאגׄזא אלסוד בחיתׄ כאנת או באיגׄאד אלביאץׄ פי אלהוא פי זמאן אלאור ואעדאמה באיגׄאד אלסואד פי מחלה פי זמאן אלחשך פיחצל אלפצל בין אלזמאנין כדׄלך. ואלהבדלה פי אלעבראני תנקסם אקסאמא א׳ מא תקדם דׄכרה מן אלזמאנין וכקו׳ להבדיל בין היום ובין הל׳ (בראשית א:יד) ותׄאניהא אלפצל בין גׄסמין בגׄעל גׄסם תׄאלתׄ בינהמא כקו׳ והבדילה הפרכת לכם בין הקדש ובין
content.english: ...to certain quarters and [thereby] making the black particles [appear] where they were, or by the bringing-into-existence of whiteness in the air at the time of light and its annulling [it] by the bringing-into-existence of blackness in its locus at the time of darkness, so that the separation between the two times comes about in this manner. And "separation"¹ in Hebrew divides into [several] categories²: first, the [sense] just mentioned, of [separating] the two times — and as in His words le-havdil bein ha-yom u-vein ha-l[aylah] "to separate between the day and the night" (Gen 1:14); and second, separation between two bodies by the placing of a third body between them, as in his words ve-hivdilah ha-parokhet lakhem bein ha-qodesh u-vein...
content.comments: ¹ al-habdalah (ההבדלה) — Hebrew preserved verbatim as the topic-term; the morphological category being analyzed. ² aqsām (أقسام) — "categories, divisions"; sing. qism. Standard Karaite analytical partition.

content.hebrew: קדש הקדשים (שמות כו:לג). ויבדל בין המים אשר מתחת לרקיע וג׳ (בראשית א:ז). ותׄאלתׄהא מא מענאה אפראד אלשי מן גירה ופצלה ענה באלאבעאד ואלמבאינה̈ כקו׳ והוא יבדיל מקהל הגולה (עזרא י:ח) הבדל יבדילני ייי מעל עמו (ישעיה נו:ג) ומאי גׄרי הדׄא אלמגׄרי ממא לא יקאל פיה בין כדׄא וכדׄא בל תדכׄל אלמים עלי אלאסם אלמנפצל ענה. וראבעהא מא מענאה תמייז אלשי מן גירה באמר מכׄצוץ מע אכׄתלאפה כקו׳ שלש ערים תבדיל לך (דברים יט:ב) אז יבדיל משה שלש ערים (דברים ד:מא). ואבדיל אתכם מן העמים (ויקרא כ:כו). להבדיל בין הקדש ובין החול (ויקרא י:י)[2] ואשבאה דׄלך.
content.english: ...qodesh ha-qodashim "and the curtain shall separate for you between the holy [place] and the holy of holies" (Exod 26:33), "and let it separate between the waters which are below the firmament," etc. (Gen 1:7). Third, [the sense] whose meaning is the singling out of a thing apart from another and separating it [from it] by [way of] distancing and disjunction¹, as in his words ve-hu yivdil mi-qehal ha-golah "and he shall be separated from the assembly of the exile" (Ezra 10:8) [and] havdel yavdilenī YHWH me-ʿal ʿammo "the LORD will surely separate me from His people" (Isa 56:3). And whatever runs the course² of this — anything in which one does not say bein kadhā wa-kadhā "between such-and-such and such-and-such," but rather the mim³ enters upon the noun that is separated [from the subject]. And fourth, [the sense] whose meaning is the distinguishing⁴ of a thing from another by some particular matter despite its differing [from it], as in his words shalosh ʿarim tavdil lakh "three cities you shall set apart for yourself" (Deut 19:2), az yavdil Moshe shalosh ʿarim "then Moses set apart three cities" (Deut 4:41), ve-avdil etkhem min ha-ʿammim "and I have separated you from the peoples" (Lev 20:26), le-havdil bein ha-qodesh u-vein ha-ḥol "to separate between the holy and the common" (Lev 10:10) [2] and the like.
content.comments: ¹ al-mubāyana (المباينة) — "disjunction, distinct separation"; technical pairing with al-ibʿād ("distancing"). ² See glossary s.v. yajrī majrā. ³ al-mīm (المים) — Ali's name for the Hebrew preposition prefix מ (= "from"), parallel to his hāʾ al-taʿrīf for the article ה. ⁴ tamyīz (تمييز) — "distinguishing, marking off"; in formal nahw also "specifier," but here in the lexical sense of drawing a distinction.

content.hebrew: Gen 1:5
content.english: Gen 1:5

content.hebrew: ויקרא אלהים לאור יום – יעני סמי זמאן אלנור נהארא וזמאן אלטׄלמה̈ לילא והו מדה̈ קטע אלפלך
content.english: "And God called the light day" (va-yiqra Elohim la-or yom). That is, He named the time of light "day" and the time of darkness "night"; and that is the span of the [celestial] sphere's traversal...

content.hebrew: מן מוצׄע אלי מתׄלה פסמי בעץׄ הדׄה אלמדה̈ יום והו מא יחצל אלנור פיה ובעצׄהא לילה̈ והו מא יחצל אלטׄלאם
content.english: ...from a [given] position to its like. Then some of this span He named yom ("day") — namely [the portion] in which light obtains — and some of it laylah ("night") — namely [the portion] in which darkness obtains...

content.hebrew: פיה. תׄם ערף אסם הדׄין אלזמאנין בקו׳ ויהי ערב ויהי בקר יום (בראשית א:ה) פאלערב אסם לאול אלליל ואלבקר אסם לאול ומענאה פצאר אלזמאן אלדׄי אולה ערב ואלזמאן אלדׄי אולה בקר יומא ואחדא פהדׄא הו אליום אללגוי אלגׄאמע ללליל ואלנהאר. ואמא אליום אלשרעי פקד יכון עלי בעץׄ הדׄה אלמדה̈ כקו׳ שבעת ימים תהיה בנדתה (ויקרא טו:יט) אלתי קד יכון פיהא מא הו סאעה̈ ואסמאה יום ויגׄוז כון אלערב ואלבקר אלחאצלין פי אלתׄלתׄה̈ איאם קבל כׄלק אלשמס אדׄ גׄסם אלאור אלמקול ענה יהי אור (בראשית א:ג) קד גׄעל מגׄרי אלשמס פי אלאנארה̈ ואלאסתצׄא בה.
content.english: ...in it. Then He identified the name of these two times by His words va-yhi ʿerev va-yhi voqer yom [eḥad] "and there was evening and there was morning, one day" (Gen 1:5). For ʿerev is the name of the beginning of night, and voqer is the name of the beginning [of day], and its meaning is: the time whose beginning is evening, and the time whose beginning is morning, [together amount to] one day. So this is the lexical¹ day [in the broad sense] that comprises [both] the night and the [daytime]. As for the legal² day [in the technical sense], it may [apply] to [only] part of this span — as in His words shivʿat yamim tihyeh ve-nidatah "seven days she shall be in her [state of] impurity" (Lev 15:19), in which there may be [a unit] that is [only] an hour, and He calls it "day." And it is admissible that the evening and the morning that obtain in the three days prior to the creation of the sun [be of this nature], since the body of light of which it is said yehi or "let there be light" (Gen 1:3) had been put in the place of the sun in giving illumination and being illumined by.
content.comments: ¹ lughawī (لغوي) — "lexical, [pertaining to ordinary] language"; the everyday-language sense of a term. ² sharʿī (شرعي) — "legal, [pertaining to] revealed Law"; the technical sense as governed by the halakhic context. The pair lughawī / sharʿī is a standard Karaite analytic distinction.

content.hebrew: ואעלם אנה קד קיל אן ערב יקע עלי גׄמלה̈ אלליל כקו׳ אם שכבתי ואמרתי מתי אקיץ ומדד ערב (איוב ז:ד). יעני בה גׄמלה̈ אלליל כאן יקול פיה לשדה̈ מרצׄה כקולה ושבעתי נדודים עדי נשף (איוב ז:ד). פאן כאן דׄלך כדׄלך פהו שדׄ ואלמשהור כון ערב עלי אלוקת אלמכׄצוץ אלדׄי אולה עקיב תקצׄי אלנהאר והו אול אלליל אלי מגיב נור אלשמס פיפעל פיה מא אפתרץׄ עמלה פיה מן דׄבח אלפסח כקו׳ שם תזבח את הפסח בערב (דברים טז:ו) ומא סוי דׄלך פאמא אלבקר פקד וקע עלי אוקאת מתגאירה̈ אחדהא מא הו קבל אלפגׄר כקו׳ ויתעללו בה כל הלילה עד הבקר וישלחוה כעלות השחר (שופטים יט:כה). ותׄאניהא מא הו ענד אשראק אלשמס כקו׳ והיה בבקר כזרח השמש (שופטים ט:לג). וכאור בקר יזרח שמש (שמואל ב׳ כג:ד). ותׄאלתׄהא מא הו בין הדׄין אלוקתין אעני בין אלשחר ובין זריחת השמש כקו׳ ויהי בבקר כעלות המנחה (מלכים ב׳ ג:ב) לאנה יקרב אנה עני בדׄלך אלתמיד פחצל אלבקר יקע עלי תׄלתׄה אוקאת כמא אן אלערב איצׄא יקע עלי ג׳ אוקאת א׳ מגיב
content.english: And know that it has been said¹ that ʿerev [may] fall upon the totality of the night, as in his words im shakhavtī ve-amartī matay aqūm u-madad ʿarev "when I lie down and say, 'When shall I arise?' and [the night] stretches on as evening" (Job 7:4) — by which is meant the totality of the night: as if he were saying this on account of the severity of his sickness, like his words ve-savaʿtī nedudim ʿadei nashef "and I am full of tossings till twilight" (Job 7:4). But if that be so, it is anomalous²; the well-known [use] is that of ʿerev applying to the specific time whose beginning is just after the close of the daytime — that is, the start of the night until the setting of the sun's light — and in it is performed what was obligated to be done in it, [namely] the slaughter of the Passover [offering], as in his words sham tizbaḥ et ha-pesaḥ ba-ʿerev "there shall you sacrifice the Passover [in the] evening" (Deut 16:6), and the like. As for voqer, it falls upon distinct times: one of them is [the time] before dawn, as in his words va-yitʿalelu vah kol ha-laylah ʿad ha-boqer va-yeshalleḥuah ke-ʿalot ha-shaḥar "and they abused her all the night until the morning, and they let her go when the dawn arose" (Judg 19:25); the second is [the time] at the rising of the sun, as in his words ve-hayah va-boqer ki-zroaḥ ha-shemesh "and it shall be in the morning, when the sun rises" (Judg 9:33), [and] u-khe-or boqer yizraḥ shamesh "and like the light of morning the sun shall rise" (2 Sam 23:4); the third is [the time] between these two times — I mean between the dawn and the rising of the sun — as in his words va-yhi va-boqer ka-ʿalot ha-minḥah "and it was in the morning, at the time of the offering of the meal-offering" (2 Kgs 3:20)³, since it is plausible⁴ that he meant by that [the time of] the daily offering (tamid). So [the term] voqer falls upon three [distinct] times, just as ʿerev too falls upon three [distinct] times. [The] first [is the] setting...
content.comments: ¹ See glossary s.v. qīla. ² shādhdh (شاذّ) — "anomalous, aberrant"; the technical Karaite term for a usage that departs from the well-known (mashhūr) norm. Ali rates this view as anomalous against the standard sense. ³ The citation in source is tagged מלכים ב׳ ג:ב, but the locus of the phrase va-yhi va-boqer ka-ʿalot ha-minḥah is 2 Kgs 3:20 (and parallel ʿalot ha-minḥah at 1 Kgs 18:36); rendered as 2 Kgs 3:20 per scriptural attestation. ⁴ yaqrub (يقرب) — "it is plausible"; pairs with yabʿud / baʿīd. Marks an inferential, non-decisive judgment.

content.hebrew: גׄרם אלשמס כקו׳ נפש אשר תגע בו וטמאה עד הערב (ויקרא כב:ו) וקאל ובא השמש וטהר (ויקרא כב:ז). ואלאכׄר מגיב נור אלשמס כקו׳ בין הערבים (שמות יב:ו) אלדׄי דׄלך מן אלפאטׄ אלתתׄניה̈ מתׄל עינים ורגלים וגיר דׄלך פחצל מעני ערבים ערב אול וערב תׄאני וכאן אלאולי גׄעל אלאול מגיב גׄרם אלשמס. ואלתׄאני
content.english: [of the] body of the sun, as in his words nefesh asher tigʿa bo ve-ṭamʾah ʿad ha-ʿerev "a soul which touches it shall be unclean until evening" (Lev 22:6), and he said u-va ha-shemesh ve-ṭaher "and the sun sets and he is clean" (Lev 22:7); and the second [is the] setting of the sun's light, as in his words bein ha-ʿarbayim "between the [two] evenings" (Exod 12:6) — that being one of the lexical forms of the dual¹, like ʿeinayim ("[two] eyes") and raglayim ("[two] feet") and the like. So the sense of ʿarbayim [is] a first evening and a second evening, and the most appropriate [reading] is to take the first as the setting of the body of the sun, and the second...
content.comments: ¹ alfāẓ al-tathniya (ألفاظ التثنية) — "[lexical] forms of the dual"; the standard Karaite categorization of Hebrew dual forms by reference to the Arabic dual number.

content.hebrew: מגיב נורהא והו אלשפק אלדׄי בעדה תטׄלם גׄהה̈ אלגרב ואלערב אלג׳ פהו בין הדׄין כקו׳ שם תזבח את הפסח
content.english: ...as the setting of its light — namely the twilight-glow¹ after which the western quarter darkens; and the third ʿerev is [the one situated] between these two, as in his words sham tizbaḥ et ha-pesaḥ...
content.comments: ¹ al-shafaq (الشفق) — "the twilight afterglow"; the standard Arabic astronomical-cosmological term for the residual brightness after sunset.

content.hebrew: בערב (דברים טז:ו) וקאל ען הדׄא אלוקת ושחטו אתו כל קהל עדת ישראל בין הערבים (שמות יב:ו). יעני אלפסח פסמי וקת דׄבחה ערב מתוסטא בין הערבים והו מן עקיב מגיב גׄרם אלשמס אלי חין מגיב נורהא וקתא ואסעא ותם פיה דׄבח בהאים כתׄירה̈.
content.english: ...ba-ʿerev "in the evening" (Deut 16:6), and he said concerning this time ve-shaḥaṭu oto kol qehal ʿadat Yisraʾel bein ha-ʿarbayim "and the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall slaughter it between the [two] evenings" (Exod 12:6) — meaning the Passover [offering]. So the time of its slaughter was named ʿerev as situated between the [two] evenings; and this is from immediately after the setting of the body of the sun until the setting of its light — a broad time-span, in which the slaughter of many animals took place.

content.hebrew: Gen 1:2
content.english: Gen 1:2

content.hebrew: – וקו׳ אחד – בעד קולה יום הו עלי טריק אסתעמאל אללגה̈ תאכידא ולאנה יריד יקול בעדה יום שני ושלישי וגירהמא והדׄא אול אלסתה̈ אלמסמאאת אלתי סמאהא תע׳ פי זמאן אלכׄליקה̈ והי אור סמאה יום. חשך סמאה לילה. רקיע סמאה שמים. יבשה סמאהא ארץ. מקוה המים סמאהא ימים ומא קאל פיה ויקרא את שמם אדם (בראשית ה:ב).
content.english: "one" (eḥad). After His saying yom ["day"], it is by way of customary usage of the language¹, for emphasis², and because He intends to say after it yom sheni and shelishi and others. And this is the first of the six named [items] that He (may He be exalted) named in the time of the creation — namely [these]: or He named yom, ḥoshekh He named laylah, raqiaʿ He named shamayim, yabashah He named ereṣ, miqveh ha-mayim He named yamim, and that of which he said va-yiqra et shemam Adam "and He called their name Adam" (Gen 5:2).
content.comments: ¹ ʿalā ṭarīq istiʿmāl al-lughah (على طريق استعمال اللغة) — "by way of the customary use of the language"; the locution is the natural idiom and is not redundant or grammatically problematic. ² taʾkīdan (تأكيدا) — "for emphasis"; the standard Karaite functional category, parallel to Arabic taʾkīd / tawkīd.

content.hebrew: Gen 1:6
content.english: Gen 1:6

content.hebrew: ויאמר אלהים יהי רקיע – קד תקדם מעני ויאמר פי ויאמר אלהים יהי אור (בראשית א:ג).
content.english: "And God said, 'Let there be a firmament'" (va-yomer Elohim yehi raqiaʿ). The meaning of va-yomer has already preceded at va-yomer Elohim yehi or "and God said, 'Let there be light'" (Gen 1:3).

content.hebrew: וקו׳ יהי – מענאה אלחדתׄ חסב מא מצׄי פי יהי אור (בראשית א:ג).
content.english: "Let there be" (yehi). Its meaning is [the bringing-about of] the event¹, in accordance with what has gone by at yehi or (Gen 1:3).
content.comments: ¹ al-ḥadath (الحدث) — "event, [verbal] action"; the bare verbal-event meaning, here understood as God's act of bringing the firmament into being.

content.hebrew: – וקולה רקיע – יפסר בסאטא לכונה מנבסטא עלי אלעאלם כקו׳ תרקיע עמו לשחקים (איוב לז:יג) והו מן אמתׄלה̈ פעיל במעני מפעול לכונה מתעדיא אדׄ משהור מא לא יתעדי מן אלפעל כון פעילה במעני פאעל נחו לא יעשר (איוב טו:כט) ולא יצערו (ירמיהו ל:יט) אלדׄין המא פעלאן גיר מתעדיין גׄא פעילהמא במעני פאעל נחו עשיר ורש (משלי כב:ב) צעיר אני לימים (איוב לב:ו) אלדׄין מענאהמא עושר וצוער ליגׄאא עלי מקתצׄא קיאס אמסא אלפאעלין מן אוזאן הדׄה אלאפעאל ואלפעל אלמתעדי יגׄי משהור פעילה במתׄאבה̈ אלמפעול נחו וימשח אתו (שמואל א׳ טז:יג) אלדׄי יגׄי מנה אסם אלפאעל מושח ואלמפעול משוח חסב מא תקתצׄיה אוזאנה וכדׄלך ורקע ברגלך (יחזקאל ו:יא) יגׄי פאעלה רוקע ומפעולה רקוע קיאסא פגׄא אלמפעולאן אלתסמיה̈ ללרקיע מן קבלה תע׳ כתסמיה̈ אלמסמיאת פי אלשרע נחו עלה וחטאת וגירהמא פאן פרקא בין אלתסמיתין מין חיתׄ אן אלאסמא אלוארדה̈ פי מעשה בראשית לא תפיד פעלא מן קבלנא כלפנאה בל תגׄרי מגׄרי אלמואצׄעה̈ אללגויה̈ אלתי יפהמא אהל אללגה̈ בעצׄהם ען בעץׄ ענד אבתדי אלאצטלאח למא ראי פי דׄלך מן אלצלאח והו אסם גיר מפיד גׄארי מגׄרי אללקב וקד יגׄוז מע דׄלך אלתכׄאטב בהדׄא אלאסם פימא בעד עוצׄא מן אלאסם אלאכׄר חסב מא ראינאה פי אלבעץׄ מנהא כקו׳ את הים ואת היבשה (יונה א:ט). ויבשת ידיו יצרו (תהלים צה:ה). וליס כדׄלך אלאסמא אלשרעיה̈ מן חיתׄ אנהא תקתצׄי אפעאלא כלפהא אלמכלף פיהא לא יחסן תסמיתהא בהא אלא בעד אחדאתׄ תלך אלאפעאל פיהא כקו׳ אם עלה קרבנו (ויקרא א:ג). תׄם שרח אלאפעאל אלמאמור בהא מן קו׳ זכר תמים יקריבנו (ויקרא א:ג) וגירה סמאהא בעד דׄלך עלה כקו׳ עלה הוא (ויקרא א:יג) פלא יגׄוז תסמיתהא בגיר עלה מע אלאפעאל אלמדׄכורה̈ פיהא ומע תׄבות אלשרע כמא גׄאז תסמיה̈ אלארץׄ יבשה.
content.english: "And his saying 'firmament'" (raqiaʿ). It is glossed as "a [thing] spread out"¹ on account of its being spread² over the world, as in His words tarqiaʿ ʿimmo li-shḥaqim "[were you with Him] in spreading out for Him the skies" (Job 37:18). And it is among the patterns of faʿīl in the sense of mafʿūl³, because it [the verb r-q-ʿ] is transitive — since well-known is [the fact that] [a verb] that is not transitive, its faʿīl-form is in the sense of fāʿil⁴, like lo yeʿasher "he shall not grow rich" (Job 15:29) and lo yiṣʿaru "they shall not be brought low" (Jer 30:19), which are two intransitive verbs whose faʿīl came in the sense of fāʿil — like ʿashir va-rash "rich and poor" (Prov 22:2), ṣaʿir ani la-yamim "I am young in days" (Job 32:6), the meanings of which two [forms] are ʿosher and ṣoʿar⁵ — coming on the demand⁶ of the analogical rule⁷ of the morphological active patterns⁸ from the [verbal] structures of these verbs.
